about: Word families: one English word, several original words. Each member's anchor verse is checked by build/build-data.mjs (the WEB text must contain the member's English word), and every Strong's id must exist in the offline dictionary. Add a family here whenever a chapter meets an English word that hides more than one Greek or Hebrew word.

families.name: Power, Strength & Authority
families.intro: English Bibles say ‘power’ for at least six different Greek words. Paul stacks four of them in one breath in Ephesians 1:19 and lists four ranks of spiritual power in Ephesians 1:21. In Colossians 1:13 the WEB's ‘power of darkness’ is not δύναμις at all but ἐξουσία — authority. Knowing which word stands behind ‘power’ tells you what kind of power is meant.

members.sense: Inherent ability — the capacity to act and to accomplish. Also used for miracles (‘mighty works’), because a miracle is power on display.
To empower, to strengthen inwardly — to put δύναμις into someone; Christ enabling His servants.
Power in operation — energy actually being exerted. Used in the New Testament almost only of God's (or Satan's) power at work.
To be at work, to operate effectively — the verb of ἐνέργεια: God's power actively working in His people and His word.
Dominion-strength — power that prevails and rules. Often in doxologies: to Him be the power forever.
Strength, force, might — the raw capacity a person possesses, as in loving God with all your strength.
Authority — the right to act, delegated or given. Not how strong you are, but what you are authorised to do.
Rule, principality — a position of first rank (also means ‘beginning’). Used for ruling powers, human and spiritual.
Ruler, sovereign — one who holds δύναμις; God as the only absolute Sovereign.

The authority of a command — an order given with the right to give it. In Titus 2:15 the WEB renders it ‘authority’, but it is not ἐξουσία: it is the weight of God’s commandment behind the teacher (the same word is ‘commandment’ in Titus 1:3).
Active, effective, at work — the adjective of ἐνέργεια: God’s word is not inert but operating.
To be made strong, empowered — from δύναμις: the heroes of faith ‘from weakness were made strong’ (Hebrews 11:34).
Strong, mighty — the adjective of ἰσχύς: physical or moral strength (Hebrews 11:34 ‘mighty in war’).
To be able, to have power to — the everyday verb of the δύναμις family.
To have strength, to prevail — force exercised.
Mighty — strong with ruling might, the adjective of κράτος.
To strengthen — to make strong in body and resolve.
Lordship, dominion — the authority of a lord.

families.name: Signs, Wonders & Mighty Works
families.intro: The New Testament describes miracles with three words, often together: δύναμις (a mighty work — the power behind it), σημεῖον (a sign — what it points to) and τέρας (a wonder — the amazement it causes). God attested Jesus with all three (Acts 2:22). 2 Thessalonians 2:9 warns that the lawless one will counterfeit all three: ‘power and signs and lying wonders’.

members.sense: Mighty work — a miracle seen as an act of power.
Sign — a miracle seen as pointing beyond itself, revealing who is at work (John's word for Jesus' miracles).
Wonder, portent — a miracle seen as something astonishing; never used alone of Jesus' miracles in the New Testament.

families.name: Time, Season & Age
families.intro: Greek separates kinds of time that English blurs together. Acts 1:7 sets ‘times’ (χρόνος) beside ‘seasons’ (καιρός): length of time and the right moment. In John 17:1 the WEB's ‘the time has come’ is ὥρα, the appointed hour. Two adverbs built on καιρός, εὐκαίρως and ἀκαίρως, set the favourable moment against the unfavourable one in 2 Timothy 4:2. Hebrews adds σήμερον, ‘today’: the present day of opportunity.

members.sense: Chronological time — duration, a span of time, time as it passes (the root of ‘chronology’).
The right moment — a season, an opportunity, a decisive time that must be seized.
‘Well-timed’ — εὐ (good) + καιρός: at a convenient, opportune moment, when the season is favourable.
‘Ill-timed’ — ἀ (not) + καιρός: at an inconvenient, unfavourable moment. Paired with εὐκαίρως, it means ‘whether the moment suits or not’.
Hour — literally an hour, and in John the appointed hour of Jesus' death and glory.
Age, era — a long period with its own character (‘this present evil age’), and in the plural, eternity.
Day — a literal day, and ‘the day’ of the Lord's return and judgment.
Well-timed — εὖ + καιρός: help that arrives at exactly the right moment.
For a season, temporary — πρός + καιρός: lasting only for a time, like the ‘pleasures of sin for a time’ Moses refused (Hebrews 11:25).
Today — this very day. In Hebrews it is the day of opportunity to hear God’s voice (3:7–4:11), and the ‘today’ of Christ who is the same yesterday, today and forever (13:8).
To take time, delay — from χρόνος: ‘he will not wait’ (Hebrews 10:37).
A year — a full cycle of time.
Tomorrow — the next day, which no one controls.
Eternal — belonging to the age to come, without end.
A year — a count of years.

families.name: Love & Affection
families.intro: In John 21:15 Jesus asks with ἀγαπάω and Peter answers with φιλέω; the WEB marks the difference as ‘love’ and ‘affection’. The common Greek word ἔρως (romantic desire) never appears in the New Testament. 2 Timothy 3:2–4 adds a row of φιλ- compounds — lovers of self, of money, of pleasure, rather than lovers of God: love itself misdirected. Titus adds the bright side of the φιλ- compounds: lover of good, of guests, of husband and children — and God’s own φιλανθρωπία, His love toward mankind.

members.sense: To love by choice and commitment — self-giving love that seeks the other's good, the love God shows.
Love (noun) — the self-giving love described in 1 Corinthians 13 and poured out by God.
To be fond of, have warm affection for — the love of friends (φίλος, friend).
Brotherly love — the warm love of brothers and sisters, applied to the family of believers.
Tenderly affectionate — the natural, family kind of love (στοργή) between relatives.
Lover of self — φίλος + αὐτός: love turned inward, the first mark of the last days.
Lover of money — φίλος + ἄργυρος, silver: love fastened on wealth.
Not a lover of good — hostile to what is good; love withdrawn from goodness.
Lover of pleasure — φίλος + ἡδονή: love that lives for enjoyment.
Lover of God — the love that should rule all others, and the one the last days replace with pleasure.
‘Lover of good’ — φίλος + ἀγαθός: one who delights in goodness and good people. The opposite of ἀφιλάγαθος (2 Timothy 3:3).
‘Lover of strangers’ — φίλος + ξένος: hospitable, opening home and table to guests.
‘Husband-loving’ — φίλος + ἀνήρ: warm, devoted affection of a wife for her husband.
‘Child-loving’ — φίλος + τέκνον: a parent’s tender affection for their children.
‘Love of humankind’ (the root of ‘philanthropy’): kindness toward people as people. Titus 3:4 uses it of God Himself.
‘Love of strangers’ — hospitality: opening home and table to guests (Hebrews 13:2; the noun of φιλόξενος).
‘Not a lover of money’ — free from greed; the opposite of φιλάργυρος.
Beloved — one who is loved with ἀγάπη.
A friend — one who is loved with φιλία, warm personal affection.
Friendship — warm personal affection and loyalty.
Loving as brothers — warm family affection for fellow believers.
Friendly-minded, courteous — kindly disposed towards others.
A kiss — the sign of affection (from φιλέω).

families.name: Mercy & Compassion
families.intro: Two Greek families stand behind ‘mercy’ and ‘compassion’. ἔλεος / ἐλεέω is mercy that acts — help given to those in need or misery, pardon to the guilty. οἰκτιρμός / οἰκτίρμων / οἰκτίρω is pity, the tender feeling of compassion. And σπλάγχνα words (σπλαγχνίζομαι, πολύσπλαγχνος) speak of compassion felt in the gut — being moved inside. Romans 9:15 sets ἐλεέω and οἰκτίρω side by side, and James 5:11 calls the Lord πολύσπλαγχνος and οἰκτίρμων, ‘full of compassion and mercy’.

members.sense: Mercy — compassion that acts to help the needy or pardon the guilty.
To have mercy, to show mercy in word or deed.
To have compassion, to feel pity.
Pity, mercies — the tender compassions of God.
Compassionate, merciful — full of tender pity.
Very compassionate — literally ‘many-bowelled’, deeply moved within.
To be moved with compassion — to feel it in the gut.
Sympathetic — feeling with another, suffering alongside.
Tender-hearted — compassionate from deep within.
The inward parts — the heart as the seat of compassion.

families.name: Know & Knowledge
families.intro: ‘Know’ in English can mean knowing a fact or knowing a person. Greek usually keeps these apart. 1 Corinthians 8:1 has both οἶδα (‘we know’) and γνῶσις (‘knowledge’) in one sentence.

members.sense: To come to know by experience and relationship — knowing a person, not just facts about them.
To know as settled fact, to perceive (Strong's files the past-tense ‘saw’ under this number too).
Knowledge — what is known; at Corinth, knowledge that puffed people up.
Full, precise knowledge — ἐπί (upon) + γνῶσις: knowledge that grips and transforms.
To know well, understand, be acquainted with — Abraham went out ‘not knowing’ where he was going (Hebrews 11:8).
To know fully, recognise — the verb of ἐπίγνωσις: knowledge that grasps and acknowledges.

families.name: Wisdom, Prudence & Understanding
families.intro: English ‘wise’ and ‘understanding’ hide several Greek words. σοφία / σοφός is wisdom in its fullest sense — insight into God’s ways and the skill to live by them. φρόνησις / φρόνιμος is practical good sense, prudence, knowing what to do in a situation (the ‘wise man’ who built on the rock, Matthew 7:24). σύνεσις is understanding, putting things together in the mind. ἐπιστήμων is the knowledgeable expert. James 3:13 asks for σοφός and ἐπιστήμων together, then insists that true wisdom is shown in conduct, not in knowledge.

members.sense: Wisdom — insight into God’s ways and the skill to live by them.
Wise — having that wisdom.
Understanding, knowledgeable — the expert who knows his subject.
Prudence — practical good sense for living.
Prudent, sensible — wise in action, like the builder on the rock.
Understanding — putting things together in the mind.

families.name: Word & Utterance
families.intro: Both λόγος and ῥῆμα are translated ‘word’. The sword of the Spirit in Ephesians 6:17 is the ῥῆμα of God — the word spoken.

members.sense: Word, message, reasoned account — and Jesus Himself, the Word.
A spoken word, an utterance — a particular saying that proceeds out of a mouth.
An oracle — an utterance of God.

families.name: Book & Scroll
families.intro: English ‘book’ hides three related Greek words. βίβλος is a written volume, a record — ‘the book of life’ (Revelation 3:5) or ‘the book of the genealogy’ (Matthew 1:1); βιβλίον, its diminutive in form but normal in use, is a scroll or written document — the sealed scroll in the hand of God (Revelation 5:1); βιβλαρίδιον is a truly little scroll, the one John is told to eat (Revelation 10:2, 9–10). In the ancient world ‘books’ were rolls of papyrus or parchment, not bound pages.

members.sense: A book, a written volume or record — especially the book of life.
A scroll, a written document; in Revelation the sealed scroll of God’s purposes.
A little scroll.

families.name: Witness & Testimony
families.intro: English ‘witness’ and ‘testimony’ hide four Greek words from one root. μάρτυς is the person who bears witness — and because so many witnesses for Jesus died for it, the word became our ‘martyr’ (Revelation 2:13; 17:6); μαρτυρία is the testimony given, the content of the witness; μαρτύριον is testimony as evidence or proof, as in ‘the tabernacle of the testimony’; and μαρτυρέω is the verb, to testify. Revelation 1:2 and 1:5 put three of them together: John testified to the testimony of Jesus Christ, the faithful witness.

members.sense: A witness — the person who testifies; by extension one who dies for the testimony, a martyr.
Testimony — the evidence or witness that is given.
Testimony as evidence or proof; used of the Law kept in the tabernacle.
To testify, to bear witness.

families.name: Life & Soul
families.intro: ‘Life’ in English Bibles can stand for three Greek words: life itself, the means of living, and the individual soul. John 10:10–11 uses two of them a sentence apart.

members.sense: Life itself — the life that comes from God; ‘eternal life’.
Livelihood, the means and course of earthly life — possessions, lifestyle.
Soul — the individual self, the person's own life (laid down by the Good Shepherd).
To live — the verb of ζωή: to be alive, with the life that comes from God.
To make alive, to give life.
To live out one’s life — the course of earthly life (βίος), as distinct from ζάω, to be alive.

families.name: Birth & New Birth
families.intro: Several Greek words lie behind ‘born’ and ‘birth’. γεννάω is the ordinary word for fathering or being born; Jesus says one must be born ἄνωθεν, ‘anew’ or ‘from above’ (John 3:3). ἀναγεννάω, ‘to beget again’, is Peter’s word for new birth (1 Peter 1:3, 23). ἀποκυέω is to bring forth from the womb — James uses it both for sin giving birth to death and for God giving birth to us by the word of truth (James 1:15, 18). τίκτω is to bear, to give birth.

members.sense: To father, to be born — the ordinary word for birth.
To beget again, to cause to be born again.
To bring forth from the womb — of sin giving birth to death, and of God giving birth to His children.
To bear, to give birth to.
Newly born — a baby just born.

families.name: Children & Little Children
families.intro: English ‘children’ and ‘little children’ hide three Greek words. τέκνον is a child as one born of a parent — family by birth (1 John 3:1, ‘children of God’). τεκνίον, its diminutive, is ‘little child’, a word of tender affection John uses for his readers (1 John 2:1, 12). παιδίον is a young child, a little one under training (1 John 2:13, 18). John moves between τεκνία and παιδία in 2:12–13 when he addresses the whole church.

members.sense: A child — one born of a parent, family by birth.
Little child — a term of tender affection.
A young child, a little one — a child still being trained.

families.name: New
families.intro: Greek has one word for ‘new in kind’ and another for ‘new in time’. ἀνακαίνωσις, ‘renewal’, is built on καινός: the Spirit makes us new in kind, not merely recent. Hebrews calls the covenant ‘new’ with both words: καινός (8:8, new in kind) and νέος (12:24, freshly given). Hebrews 10:20 adds a third word, πρόσφατος, originally ‘freshly slain’: the new way opened through Christ’s sacrifice.

members.sense: New in quality — fresh, unprecedented, of a different kind (a new creation).
New in time — recent, young (the new man, freshly come into being).
‘Renewal’ — ἀνά (again) + καινός: being made new in quality, renovated from within by the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5), the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2).
‘Freshly slain’, then simply ‘fresh, recent’ — the ‘new and living way’ opened by Christ’s death (Hebrews 10:20).

families.name: Another & Different
families.intro: Galatians 1:6–7 uses both words: a ‘different’ (ἕτερος) gospel, which is not ‘another’ (ἄλλος) gospel at all.

members.sense: Another of the same kind — Jesus promises another Counselor like Himself.
Another of a different kind — something other, different in nature.
To teach differently — teaching of a different kind (ἕτερος) from the apostolic gospel.

families.name: World, Age & Earth
families.intro: ‘World’ in English Bibles can mean the created order, humanity, the system opposed to God, an age, or the inhabited lands. Romans 12:2's ‘this world’ is αἰών — this age.

members.sense: The ordered world — creation, humanity, and often the world-system that rejects God.
The age — the present era with its values and spirit.
The inhabited earth — the civilised, populated world (often the Roman Empire).
Earth, land, ground — the physical earth or a territory.

families.name: Servant
families.intro: ‘Servant’ can translate five Greek words, each describing a different relationship of service.

members.sense: Bondservant, slave — one who belongs wholly to a master.
Servant in action — one who serves others, a minister (the root of ‘deacon’).
Assistant, attendant — originally an ‘under-rower’ taking orders from above.
Household servant — a domestic who lives in the master's house.
Public or sacred servant — one who carries out a priestly or public service.
An honoured attendant — a trusted servant in a household, the title God gave Moses (Hebrews 3:5). Contrasted with the Son who is over the house.
To serve in worship — religious service offered to God (or to what stands in His place). Different from δουλεύω (to serve as a slave) and διακονέω (to serve practically).
To serve, wait on, minister to — the verb of διάκονος: practical service of others.
Service, ministry — the practical help of a διάκονος.
To serve as a slave — the verb of δοῦλος: to be ruled by a master, whether God or desires.
To enslave — to be made a δοῦλος, owned by something (Titus 2:3, ‘enslaved to much wine’).
Slavery, bondage — the condition of a δοῦλος (fear of death as bondage, Hebrews 2:15).
Worship-service — the noun of λατρεύω: the ordered service offered to God.
A household manager, a steward — trusted with the master’s goods.

families.name: Work, Labour & Toil
families.intro: English ‘work’ and ‘labour’ cover several Greek words. 1 Thessalonians 1:3 sets ἔργον (work) beside κόπος (labour to the point of exhaustion), and 2:9 adds μόχθος (hardship) and ἐργάζομαι (working). Revelation 2:2 praises ‘works’ and ‘toil’ in a church that had left its first love.

members.sense: Work, deed — an action or task, what a person does (the root of ‘ergonomics’).
Labour, toil — hard work that wears you out; effort to the point of weariness.
To labour, to toil to weariness — the verb of κόπος, used of those who work hard in ministry.
Hardship, travail — exhausting toil with difficulty and struggle.
Labourer, worker — one who works for wages; used of gospel workers and teachers.
To work — to do a job, to earn a living by labour.
To work around — to bustle about in other people's affairs instead of doing one's own work; to be a busybody.
Busybody — ‘working around’, meddling in others' affairs; the adjective of περιεργάζομαι.
To work fully, to accomplish, to produce a result.
To work together with, to co-operate.

families.name: Sin, Transgression & Debt
families.intro: The New Testament describes sin from several angles: missing the mark, a false step, crossing a line, living without law, and owing a debt. Ephesians 2:1 uses two of these words together.

members.sense: Missing the mark — falling short of God's standard; the general word for sin.
A false step, a fall beside the path (often translated ‘trespass’ or ‘transgression’).
Transgression — stepping over a known line, breaking a stated command.
Lawlessness — living as if no law applied; rebellion against God's rule.
Unrighteousness, injustice — what is not right before God or toward people; ‘All unrighteousness is sin’.
Debt — something owed; sin pictured as an unpaid debt to God.
‘Mis-hearing’ — παρά + ἀκούω: refusing to listen, disobedience that begins with not hearing. Paired with παράβασις (stepping over the line) in Hebrews 2:2.
A sin of ignorance — wrongdoing committed without full knowledge; the ‘errors’ the high priest atoned for on the Day of Atonement.
To sin — the verb of ἁμαρτία: to miss the mark, and to keep on missing it.
Lawless — without law, living as if God’s law did not exist; the adjective of ἀνομία.
A transgressor — one who steps over a known boundary.
A sinner — one marked by sin.
Lawbreaking — acting against the law.

families.name: Test, Trial & Temptation
families.intro: English splits one Greek idea into ‘trial’ and ‘temptation’, and joins two different Greek ideas under ‘test’. πειρασμός / πειράζω is a putting to the test — it can be an outward trial God allows to strengthen faith, or an inner pull towards sin that never comes from God; context decides which. δοκίμιον / δοκιμάζω / δόκιμος is the assayer’s word: testing metal by fire to prove it genuine, and the approval that follows. James 1:2–15 uses both families side by side: the same πειρασμός can make you δόκιμος (approved) or, if your own desire takes hold of it, lead to sin.

members.sense: A putting to the test — an outward trial, or a temptation to sin; context decides.
A testing, a proving — the assay that shows what is genuine.
To test, to try; and in a bad sense, to tempt — to entice towards sin.
Untemptable — not able to be tempted; used of God alone.
To test as metal is tested, to prove, and so to approve.
Approved after testing — proven genuine, like coin that has passed the assay.
To reject after testing — to examine and declare unfit.

families.name: Endurance & Patience
families.intro: Two Greek words stand behind ‘endurance’, ‘patience’ and ‘perseverance’. ὑπομονή / ὑπομένω is ‘remaining under’ a load — steadfastness under hard circumstances, not giving way. μακροθυμία / μακροθυμέω is ‘long temper’ — being slow to give up on people or on God’s timing, the opposite of a short fuse. The WEB uses ‘perseverance’ for both in James 5:10–11: the prophets’ μακροθυμία and Job’s ὑπομονή.

members.sense: Endurance — remaining under a load without giving way.
To remain under, to endure — to stay steady through trial.
To be long-tempered, patient — slow to give up on people or on God’s timing.
Long-temper, patience, forbearance — the opposite of a short fuse.

families.name: Suffer & Suffering
families.intro: English ‘suffer’ and ‘suffering’ cover several Greek words. πάσχω / πάθημα is to undergo, to experience something painful done to you — Peter’s great word, used of Christ’s sufferings and the believer’s (1 Peter 1:11; 2:21). συμπάσχω is to suffer together with Christ (Romans 8:17). κακοπαθέω / κακοπάθεια is to endure hardship, to put up with what is bad (James 5:10, 13). First Peter uses this vocabulary more than any other letter.

members.sense: To undergo, to suffer — to experience pain done to you.
A suffering — what one undergoes, especially the sufferings of Christ.
To suffer together with — to share in Christ’s sufferings.
To endure hardship, to suffer evil.
Hardship endured — suffering borne patiently.

families.name: Evil & Malice
families.intro: English ‘evil’ hides several Greek words. κακός describes what is bad in itself — worthless, harmful in nature. πονηρός describes evil that is active and aggressive, actively doing harm; it is used of ‘the evil one’. 1 Thessalonians 5 uses both: do not repay κακός for κακός (5:15), and abstain from every form of πονηρός (5:22). φαῦλος adds a third shade: the worthless, paltry deed.

members.sense: Bad, evil in nature — worthless, harmful; what is wrong in itself.
Evil in action — malicious, actively doing harm; ‘the evil one’.
Malice — badness of heart, ill will that wants harm for others.
‘Worthless, base’ — the shabby, good-for-nothing kind of wrong: deeds that cannot stand the light (John 3:20) and accusations an opponent might make (Titus 2:8).
Badly, wrongly — the adverb of κακός.
An evildoer — one who does what is bad.
To harm, to do evil to — to injure someone.
To do evil, to do wrong.

families.name: Darkness
families.intro: English ‘darkness’ hides several Greek words. σκοτία (John’s favourite) is the state of darkness, the absence of light, often moral and spiritual; σκότος is darkness as a realm or condition, the opposite of φῶς; ζόφος is the thick, murky gloom of the underworld (2 Peter 2:4); σκοτεινός is the adjective, ‘dark, full of darkness’. 1 John 1:5–6 uses σκοτία and σκότος in consecutive verses: in God there is no σκοτία at all, so those who walk in σκότος cannot have fellowship with Him.

members.sense: Darkness as a state — the absence of light, often spiritual blindness.
Darkness as a realm or condition — the opposite of light.
Gloom, murk — the thick darkness of the underworld.
Dark, full of darkness.

families.name: Image, Form & Likeness
families.intro: English ‘image’ and ‘form’ hide several Greek words. εἰκών is a true image or portrait that shares in what it shows (Colossians 1:15); χαρακτήρ is the exact imprint a seal or die leaves (Hebrews 1:3). μορφή is the form that expresses what a thing really is (Philippians 2:6), while σχῆμα is outward appearance and ὁμοίωμα likeness. μόρφωσις can be a mere outward shape without the reality (2 Timothy 3:5).

members.sense: Image, portrait — a likeness that truly represents and shares in its original.
Exact imprint — the mark a seal or stamp leaves, matching it line for line.
Form — the outward expression of an inner, essential nature.
Likeness — resemblance, being made like something.
Outward fashion, appearance — the way something presents to the eye.
Outward shape — a form that may lack the reality (a ‘form of godliness’).
Likeness, resemblance — the word of Genesis 1:26 in the Greek Old Testament.
To shape oneself after a pattern, to be conformed to an outward mould.

families.name: Pattern, Copy & Shadow
families.intro: Hebrews explains the old covenant with a family of ‘picture’ words. τύπος is the original pattern or stamp from which copies are made (the plan shown to Moses, 8:5) — and also a ‘type’ that foreshadows (Romans 5:14). ὑπόδειγμα is a copy or sketch (8:5; 9:23), and also an example to follow or avoid (4:11). σκιά is a shadow, cast by a reality not yet seen (8:5; 10:1). ἀντίτυπον is a counterpart that corresponds to the original (9:24). παραβολή is a symbol, a comparison set alongside (9:9). Together they say: the tabernacle, priests and sacrifices were real, but they were pictures of Christ.

members.sense: Pattern, original model — the stamp from which copies are made; also a type that foreshadows.
Copy, sketch — a representation of the original; also an example.
Shadow — the outline cast by a reality not yet seen.
Counterpart — what corresponds to the original, a representation.
Symbol, comparison — something set alongside to illustrate.
A writing-copy — the letters a teacher writes for a child to trace.

families.name: Hold Fast, Keep & Guard
families.intro: English ‘hold fast’ and ‘keep’ hide several Greek words. κατέχω is to hold down, keep a firm grip so nothing slips (Hebrews 3:14; 10:23). κρατέω, from κράτος (strength), is to seize and hold with force (Hebrews 4:14). τηρέω is to keep watch over, preserve (2 Timothy 4:7 ‘I have kept the faith’). φυλάσσω is to guard like a sentry (1 Timothy 6:20). ἀντέχομαι is to cling to, hold on against opposition (Titus 1:9).

members.sense: To hold down, keep a firm grip — not letting go of what you have.
To grasp with strength, seize and retain (from κράτος).
To keep watch over, preserve, keep intact.
To guard as a sentry — protect against loss or attack.
To cling to, hold on firmly against pressure.
To guard as a garrison guards a city — to keep under protection.

families.name: Crown
families.intro: English ‘crown’ hides two different Greek objects. στέφανος is a wreath or garland — the victor’s prize at the games, the festive garland, the honour given to one who has won or served faithfully; διάδημα (our ‘diadem’) is the band of royal authority, the crown of a king. Believers are promised στέφανοι, victory wreaths (2:10; James 1:12); the dragon and the beast claim διαδήματα (12:3; 13:1) — but on the head of the Rider called Faithful and True are ‘many’ διαδήματα (19:12). στεφανόω is the verb, to crown with a wreath.

members.sense: A wreath or garland — the victor’s prize, a mark of honour and reward.
A diadem — the royal band, the crown of a ruler’s authority.
To crown with a wreath of honour or victory.

families.name: Sacrifice, Offering & Gift
families.intro: Hebrews uses a whole vocabulary of worship. θυσία is a sacrifice, usually an animal slain; προσφορά is an offering, the act of bringing something to God; ὁλοκαύτωμα is a whole burnt offering, entirely consumed; δῶρον is a gift. The verb προσφέρω, to bring near, to offer, is the priest’s work. Hebrews 10:5–8 gathers four of these words to show that all of them are fulfilled and ended in Christ’s one offering of His body.

members.sense: A sacrifice — usually a slain animal, offered to God.
An offering — what is brought near to God, the act of offering.
A whole burnt offering — wholly consumed on the altar.
A gift — an offering presented to God.
To bring near, to offer — the priest’s action.
To carry up, to offer up on the altar — used of Christ who ‘offered up himself’ once for all (Hebrews 7:27).
Atoning sacrifice — the offering that turns away wrath and covers sin.

families.name: Gift & Giving
families.intro: Several Greek words lie behind ‘gift’. δῶρον is a gift or offering presented; δωρεά is a free gift, given without payment; δώρημα is the thing bestowed; δόσις is the act of giving; χάρισμα is a gift of grace. James 1:17 puts two side by side — “every good gift (δόσις) and every perfect gift (δώρημα)” — the giving and the thing given both come from the Father.

members.sense: A giving — the act of giving, and so a gift.
A bestowment — the gift itself, the thing given.
A free gift, given without payment.
A gift of grace — undeserved and freely given.
A gift, an offering presented.
To grant as a gift, to bestow freely.

families.name: Redeem, Ransom & Buy
families.intro: English ‘redeem’ and ‘ransom’ cover several Greek words from two roots. λύτρον / λυτρόω / ἀπολύτρωσις come from λύω, to loose: a ransom is the price that sets a captive or slave free (Matthew 20:28; 1 Peter 1:18). ἀγοράζω / ἐξαγοράζω come from the ἀγορά, the market-place: to buy, and to buy out of — purchased so as to belong to a new owner (1 Corinthians 6:20; Galatians 3:13). Peter says the price was not silver or gold but “precious blood” (1 Peter 1:19).

members.sense: To ransom, to set free by paying a price.
A ransom — the price paid to free a captive.
Redemption — release secured by a ransom.
To buy in the market-place — purchased to belong to a new owner.
To buy out of, to buy back — redeemed from slavery to the law’s curse.

families.name: Godliness & Ungodliness
families.intro: ‘Godliness’ is the key word of 1 Timothy. English uses one word for two Greek ones: εὐσέβεια (well-directed reverence, devotion to God lived out in daily life) and the rarer θεοσέβεια (reverence for God). The opposite is ἀσέβεια / ἀσεβής — the absence of reverence, life lived as if God did not matter. Hebrews adds εὐλάβεια, reverent awe (‘godly fear’ in 5:7).

members.sense: Godliness — reverent devotion to God expressed in a whole way of life; the key word of the pastoral letters.
To show piety, to act reverently — godliness put into practice, beginning at home with one's own family.
Godly (adverb) — living reverently toward God, the way of life that draws persecution.
Reverence for God, God-fearing piety (used only once in the New Testament).
Ungodly — without reverence for God; living as if God did not matter.
Ungodliness — irreverence toward God; the noun of ἀσεβής, life without regard for God.
Reverent awe — careful, God-fearing reverence. Jesus was heard ‘for his godly fear’ (Hebrews 5:7); believers serve God ‘with reverence’ (12:28).
To act with reverent caution, to be moved by godly fear — the verb of εὐλάβεια (Noah, Hebrews 11:7).
Religious — devout in outward worship.
Religion — worship and its outward observance.
To act ungodly — to live without reverence for God.
Godly, devout — reverent towards God.

families.name: Humble, Lowly & Meek
families.intro: English ‘humble’ and ‘humility’ cover two Greek ideas. ταπεινός / ταπεινόω / ταπείνωσις / ταπεινοφροσύνη is lowness — low in position, or low in one’s own estimate, the opposite of being lifted up (ὑψόω). πραΰς / πραΰτης is meekness — gentle strength under control, the teachable spirit that does not fight God or demand its rights. The WEB sometimes uses ‘humility’ for πραΰτης (James 1:21) and ‘lowliness’ for ταπεινοφροσύνη (Ephesians 4:2), and Jesus calls Himself both: “gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

members.sense: Low, lowly, humble — low in position or in one’s own estimate.
To make low, to humble — and, of oneself, to take the low place.
Lowering, humiliation — being brought low.
Lowliness of mind — thinking of oneself modestly.
Meekness — gentle, teachable strength under God’s control.
Meek, gentle — strong but not self-assertive.

families.name: Resist & Oppose
families.intro: Three different Greek words lie behind ‘resist’. ἀντιτάσσομαι is a military word: to draw up one’s ranks against an enemy — God sets Himself in battle order against the proud (James 4:6). ἀνθίστημι is to stand one’s ground against an attack — believers stand against the devil (James 4:7; Ephesians 6:13). ἀντιπίπτω is to fall against, to push back against — Israel always resisted the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51). In James 4:6–7 the first two sit side by side: God opposes the proud, so the humble can withstand the devil.

members.sense: To draw up in battle order against, to oppose.
To stand against, to hold one’s ground.
To fall against, to push back against.

families.name: Sober, Sound-Minded & Self-Controlled
families.intro: English ‘sober’ and ‘self-control’ hide three Greek roots. νήφω / νηφάλιος is literally not drunk — clear-headed, alert. The σώφρων family (‘a saved, sound mind’) is sanity and moderation: thinking straight about God, self and others; the healed demoniac of Mark 5:15 is σωφρονοῦντα, ‘in his right mind’. ἐγκράτεια / ἐγκρατής is mastery, strength held over one’s own desires. Titus 1:8 puts σώφρων and ἐγκρατής side by side, and Titus 2 uses the σώφρων words for every age group.

members.sense: To be sober, not intoxicated — figuratively, clear-headed and alert, especially in watching for the Lord.
Sober, temperate — free from the haze of wine and excess; circumspect.
Of sound mind — sensible, self-controlled, moderate: the mind kept safe and whole.
To be of sound mind — sane, sensible; used of the healed demoniac ‘in his right mind’.
With a sound mind — living sensibly and with restraint.
Soundness of mind — good sense, sober reasonableness.
Self-discipline — a sound, disciplined mind given by the Spirit.
To make sound-minded — to train, coach or bring someone to good sense.
Mastery over oneself — strength that holds desires in check (the Spirit’s fruit).
Self-mastered — having one’s appetites under control.

families.name: Discipline, Training & Chastening
families.intro: English varies its words for one Greek family. παιδεία / παιδεύω (from παῖς, a child) is the whole upbringing of a child — teaching, training and correction. The WEB renders it ‘chastening’ (Hebrews 12:5), ‘discipline’ (12:7), ‘punished’ (12:10) and ‘instructing’ (Titus 2:12, where grace is the trainer). γυμνάζω is athletic training (‘exercised’, 5:14; 12:11). ἐλέγχω is reproof that exposes and corrects. μαστιγόω, to scourge, is the hardest form. Hebrews 12 says God’s discipline is the proof of sonship and the path to holiness.

members.sense: Child-training — instruction and correction by a loving father; ‘discipline’.
To train a child — to teach, guide, correct; grace itself does this (Titus 2:12).
To train like an athlete — exercise by repeated practice.
To reprove — expose a fault in order to correct it.
To scourge, whip — severe correction.
A rebuke, a conviction — being exposed and corrected.

families.name: Perfect, Complete & Mature
families.intro: English ‘perfect’ usually means flawless, but the Greek τέλειος family means reaching the goal (τέλος): complete, mature, fully grown. Hebrews uses it again and again: Christ was ‘made perfect’ — fully qualified as Saviour — through suffering (2:10), and is the ‘perfecter’ of faith (12:2). The law could not bring τελείωσις (7:11). A different root, καταρτίζω / ἄρτιος, means fitted, equipped, mended; ὁλόκληρος means whole in every part.

members.sense: To bring to the goal — complete, make fully qualified, bring to maturity.
Complete, mature, full-grown — having reached the goal.
Maturity, completeness — growing up in the faith.
Completion, bringing to the goal — what the old priesthood could not achieve.
Completer — one who brings something to its goal (only in Hebrews 12:2).
To fit out, mend, equip completely — like repairing nets or setting a bone.
Fitted, fully capable — exactly suited for the task.
Whole in every part — nothing missing.
To bring to an end, to carry out fully — to fulfil a command or finish a task.
To fill full — to fulfil a word or promise by filling up its meaning.
The end, the goal — the point God is working towards.
Fully, completely — the adverb of τέλειος.
To carry through to the end, to complete, to accomplish.

families.name: Author, Pioneer & Source
families.intro: The WEB uses ‘author’ for two different Greek words in Hebrews. ἀρχηγός (2:10; 12:2) is a pioneer or leader who goes first and opens the way, a founder (Peter calls Jesus ‘the Prince of life’ with it). αἴτιος (5:9) is the cause or source: Christ is the One from whom eternal salvation comes.

members.sense: Pioneer, trailblazer, leader who goes first and opens the way.
Cause, source — the one from whom something comes.

families.name: Prayer, Asking & Intercession
families.intro: Several Greek words lie behind ‘pray’ and ‘ask’. In John 14:16 the WEB's ‘I will pray to the Father’ is ἐρωτάω — to ask, as one who speaks to the Father as an equal.

members.sense: To pray to God — prayer as worship and communion, used only of prayer to God.
Prayer (noun) — prayer as worship and communion with God, the general word for prayer.
Intercession — approaching someone, especially a king, to plead on behalf of others.
Thanksgiving — grateful prayer, giving thanks to God (the root of ‘Eucharist’).
Petition — a request rising out of a specific need.
To beg, to plead — the verb of δέησις: earnest, specific asking out of need.
To ask for something — a request from a lesser to a greater.
To ask, request — on equal footing; used of Jesus asking the Father.
To intercede — to meet with someone on another's behalf.
A suppliant’s plea — originally the olive branch held out by someone begging for mercy; earnest entreaty.
A prayer, a vow — a wish expressed to God.
To pray, to wish — to make a request of God.
A petition, a request — the thing asked for.

families.name: Sickness & Healing
families.intro: English ‘sick’ and ‘heal’ hide several Greek words. ἀσθενέω is to be weak, feeble, without strength; κάμνω is to be worn out, exhausted, weary to the point of illness. σῴζω is to save, rescue, make whole — the WEB translates it ‘heal’ in James 5:15, where bodily healing and spiritual salvation meet. ἰάομαι is to cure, to heal — the physician’s word. θεραπεύω is to tend, care for and so heal. James 5:14–16 uses four of them together.

members.sense: To be weak, feeble, without strength — sick.
To be weary, worn out — sick with exhaustion.
To save, rescue, make whole — in body and in soul.
To cure, to heal — the physician’s word, used also of healing the soul.
To tend, serve and so heal — care that restores.

families.name: Good
families.intro: Greek distinguishes what is good in its effect from what is good and beautiful to look at.

members.sense: Good in nature and effect — beneficial, doing good.
Good and beautiful — noble, excellent, attractive; the Good Shepherd.
To do good, to work what is good — ἀγαθός put into action, especially generosity.
‘Teacher of what is καλός’ — one whose life and words teach what is good and beautiful.
members.en: teachers of that which is good

members.sense: Doing good — εὖ + ποιέω: practical kindness, beneficence, one of the ‘sacrifices’ that please God (Hebrews 13:16).
Well, rightly — the adverb of καλός: doing what is fine and fitting.
Kind, gracious — good in its kindness, easy and pleasant.
To do good, to do what is right.
A well-doer — one who does what is good.
Well-doing — the practice of doing good.

families.name: See, Look & Behold
families.intro: John 20:5–8 uses three different verbs that the WEB translates ‘saw’: a glance, a careful gaze, and seeing that leads to understanding — ‘he saw and believed’. Hebrews 2:8–9 puts ὁράω and βλέπω side by side.

members.sense: To look, to see with the eyes — the simple act of seeing.
To gaze, observe carefully — watching with attention (the root of ‘theatre’).
To see and perceive — seeing that understands (Strong's files ‘saw’ and ‘know’ under one number).
To behold — looking intently and taking in what is seen.
To see with the eyes or the mind — to perceive, take in. Hebrews 2:8–9 sets it beside βλέπω: we do not yet ‘see’ (ὁράω) everything subject to Him, but we do ‘see’ (βλέπω) Jesus.
To look away from everything else and fix the eyes on one object — ‘looking to Jesus’ (Hebrews 12:2).
To observe fully, to consider attentively.
To stoop and peer in — to bend over to look closely.
To watch closely, to observe as an eyewitness.
An eyewitness — one who has seen for himself.
A look, sight — what one sees.

families.name: Appear, Reveal & Manifest
families.intro: English ‘appear’ and ‘reveal’ cover several Greek words. ἐπιφαίνω / ἐπιφάνεια is a shining-forth, like dawn breaking or a king’s arrival: Titus uses it for both comings of Christ (2:11, 13; 3:4). φανερόω is to make visible what was hidden; φαίνω, to shine or be seen; ὤφθη (from ὁράω / ὀπτάνομαι), ‘was seen’, is used of the risen Lord’s appearances; ἀποκαλύπτω is to unveil, to take the cover off. Hebrews 9:24–28 uses three of them for Christ’s three appearings: φανερόω (He ‘has been revealed’ once, v. 26), ἐμφανίζω (He now appears before God for us, v. 24) and ὤφθη/ὁράω (He ‘will appear’ a second time, v. 28).

members.sense: To shine forth upon — to dawn, to appear in a burst of light.
A shining-forth, a glorious manifestation — used of Christ’s first and second comings.
To make visible, bring into the open what was hidden.
To shine; to appear, be seen.
To be seen — the word of the resurrection appearances: ‘he was seen by’.
To unveil, take the cover off — revelation of what only God can show.
To show oneself, appear openly before someone — Christ now appearing in God’s presence on our behalf (Hebrews 9:24).
To make visible, display — from φαίνω: the terrifying ‘appearance’ at Sinai (Hebrews 12:21).
To make unseen, to vanish — the opposite of φαίνω, to appear.
Revelation, unveiling — the moment something hidden is uncovered.
Visible, evident, plain — out in the open.

families.name: Rise, Raise & Resurrection
families.intro: Two Greek verbs lie behind ‘raise’ and ‘rise’. ἐγείρω pictures waking someone up; ἀνίστημι pictures standing up again. 1 Thessalonians uses both: God ‘raised’ Jesus (1:10), Jesus ‘rose’ (4:14) and the dead in Christ will ‘rise’ (4:16). The noun ἀνάστασις, resurrection, comes from the second.

members.sense: To wake, to rouse, to raise — often God raising Jesus, as one wakes a sleeper.
To stand up, to rise again — the body standing up out of death.
Resurrection — a standing up again from the dead.

families.name: Sleep & Wakefulness
families.intro: The New Testament uses two words for ‘sleep’. κοιμάω is the gentle word for believers who have died — they will wake. καθεύδω is ordinary sleep, and in 1 Thessalonians 5 the spiritual drowsiness of those who are not ready. Its opposite is γρηγορέω, to stay awake and watch. In 5:10 Paul uses ‘wake or sleep’ to mean living or having died.

members.sense: To fall asleep — used of believers who have died, because death for them is temporary.
To sleep, lie down to rest — ordinary sleep; figuratively, spiritual drowsiness.
To stay awake, to watch — alert and ready; the opposite of spiritual sleep.
To be sleepless, keep awake — to stay alert and watchful, as leaders ‘watch on behalf of your souls’ (Hebrews 13:17).
To nod, to doze — to grow drowsy.

families.name: Rest & Relief
families.intro: Hebrews 3–4 uses several words for ‘rest’. κατάπαυσις / καταπαύω is settling down to stay — the rest of Canaan and of God’s own rest. σαββατισμός (only in Hebrews 4:9) is a Sabbath-keeping, the rest that celebrates finished work. ἀνάπαυσις / ἀναπαύω is refreshment, a break from toil (Matthew 11:28–29). ἄνεσις is relief, the loosening of pressure.

members.sense: A settling down, a place of rest — the promised land and God’s own rest.
To bring to rest, to cause to settle; also to cease from work.
A Sabbath-keeping — the rest that remains for the people of God.
Refreshment, a pause from labour.
To give rest, refresh; to take one’s rest.
Relief — loosening, release from pressure or affliction.

families.name: Names and Titles of God
families.intro: The Old Testament uses several names and titles for God, and English Bibles often hide them behind ‘LORD’, ‘Lord’ and ‘God’. The WEB writes the personal name as ‘Yahweh’.

members.sense: Yahweh — God's personal covenant name (written ‘LORD’ in most English Bibles).
Elohim — God, the mighty Creator; plural in form, used with singular verbs for the one true God.
El — God, the Mighty One; often in compound titles (El Shaddai, El Elyon).
Adonai — Lord, Master; God as sovereign owner.
Tsevaot — armies, hosts; ‘Yahweh of Armies’, commander of heaven's forces.
Shaddai — the Almighty; God all-sufficient.

families.name: Sin, Iniquity & Transgression
families.intro: Hebrew has three main words for wrongdoing, and Psalm 32:5 uses all three in one verse: sin, iniquity and transgressions.

members.sense: Sin — missing the mark; also the sin offering that deals with it.
Iniquity — twistedness, perversity, and the guilt it carries.
Transgression — rebellion, deliberate revolt against God's authority.

families.name: Love, Kindness & Compassion
families.intro: Hebrew describes God's love from several angles: choosing love, covenant loyalty, womb-deep compassion and undeserved favour. Zechariah 7:9 puts kindness and compassion side by side.

members.sense: To love — to choose and hold dear (God's love for Israel).
Love (noun) — affection, the love God quietly rests in over His people.
Chesed — steadfast, loyal covenant love; kindness that keeps its promises.
Compassion — tender mercy; related to the word for womb.
Grace, favour — kindness shown to the undeserving.

families.name: Strength & Might
families.intro: Zechariah 4:6 sets two Hebrew strength-words against the Spirit: ‘Not by might, nor by power’.

members.sense: Might — force, army, wealth; the strength of resources and numbers.
Power — personal strength, the ability to do.
Mighty one — a warrior, a hero; God as champion.
To be strong — to take hold, be firm, be courageous.
Strength — might, security, stronghold.

families.name: Time, Day & Forever
families.intro: Hebrew distinguishes the season for something, the day, the appointed time and the long age.

members.sense: Time, season — the right time for something.
Day — a literal day, and ‘the day of Yahweh’.
Appointed time — a fixed meeting or feast.
Olam — age, long duration, forever.
